line: I walk out to the flat stone mid-ford and wait there with my hands empty and the pendant bright at my throat, the psalter tucked under my arm in plain sight. When the wagon stops on the bank, I call across the water, calm and clear enough for Hob and the villagers to hear. "Master Tallowmere, you wrote to me, so you can come to me. Bring your own two feet and leave Garrow on the bank."

input.add_to_description: Day 5, 5:20 PM: Met Wren mid-ford at Ashby Weir. Tall, silver-haired, clove-and-ink scent, warm voice, a lantern-topped cane. Ordered Garrow to stay on the bank and did so, smiling. Wren's Insight (12) read him as grieved and sincere, but she cannot tell whether that is real or craft. He glanced once at the pendant at her throat and went still.

entries.text:
Your voice carries over the water, and the bank goes quiet. Hob takes his pipe from his mouth. In the willows, you know, Alder and Kit are holding their breath.

The wagon stops with a creak, the painted lantern swinging. The driver stays on the box. Garrow halts at the verge, and his smile flickers when Corvin lifts two fingers without looking at him. Then Corvin Tallowmere climbs down.

He looks as you remember him: tall, silver-haired, in a good grey coat, a cane topped with a little brass lantern in his hand. The scent of clove and ink reaches you before he does. He picks his way out along the stepping stones unhurriedly, like a man crossing his own garden, and stops a few paces from your stone with the river rushing between you.

"Wren," he says. His voice is as warm as ever, and it still gets under your ribs. "You look well. Thinner." His eyes drop to your throat and the silver lantern there, and for a moment he goes completely still. Your Insight check was a 12. It tells you he looks grieved, truly, but you can't tell whether the grief is real or the finest work he's ever done.

"You opened the coffer," he says quietly. "Then you know why I wrote what I wrote. I'd hoped to tell you myself." He nods at the psalter under your arm. "Shall we speak as family, in the open as you like, or would you rather the villagers hear everything, Elowen included?"

He waits, cane planted on the wet stone. Garrow watches from the bank. The light is going gold on the water, and about forty minutes of dusk remain.

What does Wren say or do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 5, ~5:25 PM: arrives at Ashby Weir ford by wagon; appearance: tall, silver-haired, in a plum coat, soft-voiced, with a staff topped by a small brass lantern. Agreed to walk onto the mid-ford stone alone at Wren's call; told Garrow to stay on the bank. Opened by calling Wren "my girl" and glancing at the pendant, which visibly shook him.

entries.text:
You stand on the flat stone with the water running cold and quick on either side, the psalter under your arm and the pendant bright at your throat. Behind you on the bank, Hob's pipe-smoke drifts, and a dozen villagers hold the shore in uneasy silence. In the willows, you know, Alder and Kit are waiting.

The wagon creaks to a halt on the far bank. The driver stays on the box. Garrow, in his brown coat, steps down and stands with his arms folded, and his smile is gone for once.

Your voice carries clear across the water. For a long moment nobody answers. Then the canvas flap lifts and Corvin Tallowmere climbs down.

He is as you remember: tall, silver-haired, in a plum coat that is a little too fine for the road, with a staff topped by a small brass lantern. His eyes find you, then the pendant, and something in his easy face goes still. He says a few quiet words to Garrow, who scowls but stays where he is, and Corvin comes out across the stepping stones alone, light-footed, never looking down. He stops one stone short of yours.

"My girl," he says softly. "You've been busy." His gaze rests on the silver lantern. "I see you found the coffer. I did wonder if you would." He smiles, and for once it looks a little tired. "You said to come to you. Here I am. What would you have of me?"

The river hisses around the stones. The villagers are close enough to hear every word. Garrow watches from the bank, and the sun is going down behind the spur.

What does Wren say?

entries.text: dice Wren's Insight check reading Corvin as he wades out to her, DC 14: 1d20+3 = 1d20 [10] + 3 = 13

You stand on the flat stone with the river chuckling around your ankles and the psalter under your arm. Your voice carries over the water. On the bank, Hob lifts his pipe a little, and a dozen villagers go quiet.

The wagon stops at the edge of the ford. Garrow stands at the lead horse's head, smiling his thin smile. The driver stays on the box. Then the canvas curtain at the back parts, and Corvin Tallowmere climbs down.

He looks as he always did: tall, silver at the temples, a plain grey travelling coat, a voice-trained face that seems to be always about to forgive you. He rests a hand on Garrow's shoulder, says something low, and Garrow's smile thins further. But he stays. Corvin takes off his hat, hands it to the driver, and wades out alone along the stepping stones, unhurried, boots in the shallows.

Your Insight check was a 13, short of certain. You read this much. His hands are empty and he's walking carefully, but he isn't relaxed. His eyes go to the pendant at your throat and stay there a moment too long. Whatever he's feeling, it isn't the amusement he's wearing.

He stops a pace from you on the next stone, and the water runs between you. "Wren," he says warmly. "You look well. You've been busy, I hear. A whole common room." He glances at the psalter, then at the pendant, and his voice drops so only you can hear. "Where did you get that, child?"

Garrow watches from the bank. Alder and Kit are somewhere in the willows. It is nearly six, and the light is going gold.

What does Wren say?

input.add_to_description: Day 5 ~5:45 PM: appeared at the ford in a travelling cloak, silver-haired, gentle voice, clove-and-ink smell. Left Garrow and the driver on the bank. Walked onto the stepping stones alone, unarmed in view, smiling sadly. Wren's Insight (7) could not tell whether his sorrow is real.

entries.text:
You walk out along the stepping stones, the water cold and quick around them, and stop on the broad flat stone mid-ford. The psalter is under your arm and the pendant catches the last copper light. On the bank Hob puffs his pipe, and a dozen villagers stand in a wary line, still sore from noon.

The wagon halts under the willows. Your voice carries clear across the water, and for a moment nothing answers but the weir. Then a man climbs down from the box and says something short to Garrow, who stops where he is, smile fixed, hands loose. The driver stays seated.

Corvin comes alone. He is silver-haired, lean, in a travelling cloak the colour of old wine, and he steps from stone to stone with the ease of someone who has crossed a thousand rivers. He smells of clove and ink, as he always did. His hands are open and empty. When he stops a few paces from you, his face is gentle, tired and fond, and it looks like grief.

"Wren," he says softly. "You've grown thin. You've found Elowen's coffer, haven't you? I see it at your throat." He glances at the pendant, then at the psalter. "Your Insight isn't yet what I taught it to be, so I'll tell you plainly, because you've earned it. I did not kill her. But I am not clean of her either." His eyes hold yours. "Say what you came to say, child. They are listening."

Your read of him is a 7, so you can't tell whether the sorrow is real or one of his best performances.

The river runs between you, the villagers watch, and your people wait in the willows. What does Wren say?
